text: The visuals you'll use constantly, in nearly every report you ever build. Let's start with the most common one of all: the column chart, and its two close relatives.

A clustered column compares categories side by side. A stacked column shows those same categories as parts of a total, stacked on top of each other. A hundred percent stacked column goes further still, showing each category's percentage share of that total. Give any of them a real date hierarchy on the axis, and four drill icons appear. Drill up moves to a higher level. Drill down lets you select one column to see its detail. Next level expands every column at once — no clicking through one at a time.

Select a data point, and it can affect other visuals on the page two different ways. Cross-filter hides unrelated data entirely, leaving only what matches. Cross-highlight dims the rest instead, keeping the full picture visible while emphasizing your selection. Turn this on under Format, Enable interactions, then choose which behavior each connected visual should use.

And just like tables and matrices, chart colors can be entirely data-driven — a gradient here, shading lower values red and higher values blue, so performance is visible at a single glance, no legend required at all.

Line charts handle trend over a continuous axis — almost always time. Pie and donut charts handle a small part-to-whole breakdown, five or six slices at most before they get hard to read. Same underlying principles throughout, just different shapes for different questions. Next: cards, KPIs, and slicers — the visuals built for single numbers and on-canvas filtering.
